title: Heritage sites in Gujarat: Dholavira, Rani ki Vav and more
seo_title: Heritage Sites in Gujarat: UNESCO and Historical Places
meta_description: Heritage sites in Gujarat: UNESCO Dholavira, Rani ki Vav, Champaner and Ahmedabad, plus Lothal, Modhera, Girnar and Palitana, with museums and group tips.
summary: Gujarat has four UNESCO World Heritage Sites: Champaner-Pavagadh (2004), Rani ki Vav at Patan (2014), the Historic City of Ahmadabad (2017) and the Harappan city of Dholavira (2021). It also has Lothal, the Modhera Sun Temple, the Ashokan edict at Girnar, the Jain temples of Palitana and some of India's finest stepwells.

sections.h2: Why Gujarat matters for Indian heritage
paras: Gujarat has the longest coastline of any Indian state, and much of its history is about water and trade. In the 3rd millennium BCE, Harappan towns in Kachchh and Saurashtra traded shell, beads and stone. In the historic period, the ports of Bharuch and Khambhat linked western India to the Red Sea and Persian Gulf. Under the Maitrakas of Valabhi, the Chaulukyas (Solankis) of Patan and the Sultans of Gujarat, the region built temples, stepwells, mosques and cities of high quality.

The result is a state where a group can study the [Indus Valley Civilization](indus-valley-civilization.html), Solanki temple art, Indo-Islamic architecture and the colonial and modern periods in one trip.

sections.h2: UNESCO World Heritage Sites in Gujarat
paras: Dholavira (2021), on Khadir island in the Rann of Kachchh, is one of the five largest Harappan cities. It is known for its stone architecture, a citadel and city in separate walled parts, large reservoirs cut into rock, and a signboard of large Harappan signs found near the north gate. Our [Dholavira programme](dholavira-harappan-urbanism-in-kachchh.html) explains how the city managed water in a dry region.

Rani ki Vav (2014) at Patan is a stepwell built in the 11th century under the Chaulukya dynasty, traditionally in memory of King Bhima I by Queen Udayamati. It descends in seven levels and has hundreds of carved figures, many of them avatars of Vishnu. It was buried by silt and excavated by the ASI in the 20th century. See our guide to [stepwells of India](stepwells-of-india.html).

Champaner-Pavagadh (2004) combines a hill with temples and fortifications and the 15th to 16th-century city of Sultan Mahmud Begada below it, with the Jami Masjid and other mosques. The Historic City of Ahmadabad (2017), founded in 1411 by Sultan Ahmad Shah, is valued for its pols (gated residential neighbourhoods), wooden houses and its mosques and tombs. See our [heritage walk in Ahmedabad](heritage-walk-in-ahmedabad.html) guide.

Lothal, near the Gulf of Khambhat, is the best known Harappan site in the state. Its large brick basin has been read as a dockyard, though some archaeologists argue it was a water tank; both views are discussed in our session on [Lothal and Harappan trade](lothal-harappan-trade-and-its-interpretations.html). Lothal also had a bead-making workshop and a warehouse.

Other Harappan sites include Surkotada, Kanmer, Shikarpur and Gola Dhoro (Bagasra) in Kachchh, and Rangpur near Surendranagar. Vadnagar, in north Gujarat, has been excavated in recent years and shows a continuous town from about the 2nd century BCE, with a Buddhist monastery. At Junagadh, a rock at the foot of Girnar carries one of Ashoka's major rock edicts, along with later inscriptions of the Saka ruler Rudradaman and the Gupta period, which record repairs to the Sudarshana lake.

sections.h2: Ancient temples and stepwells in Gujarat
paras: The Sun Temple at Modhera (1026 to 1027), under Bhima I, has a stepped tank (Surya Kund), an assembly hall and a sanctum aligned so that the sun lights it at the equinoxes. The temple of Somnath was rebuilt many times; the present temple was completed in 1951 after independence, on the site of earlier temples. The Jain temple cities of Shatrunjaya at Palitana and on Girnar have hundreds of shrines, and the Ajitnath temple at Taranga is a fine 12th-century Solanki example.

Stepwells are a Gujarati speciality. Besides Rani ki Vav, the Adalaj stepwell (1499) and Dada Harir stepwell in Ahmedabad are easy to visit. Our [Champaner programme](champaner-pavagadh-fort-city-and-sacred-landscape.html) shows how the sultans used water in a fortified city.

The Sultans of Gujarat, who ruled from 1407 until the Mughal conquest of 1573, built one of India's most distinctive regional styles. Their mosques, such as the Jami Masjid of Ahmedabad (1424), reuse the carved pillars, brackets and domes of local temple builders inside an Islamic plan, which makes them a key case in our guide to [Indo-Islamic architecture](indo-islamic-architecture.html). Craftsmen moved between temple and mosque work, and the same families of stone carvers served both.

Later layers are worth a stop too. Surat was a major Mughal port and the site of early English and Dutch trading posts, with old Dutch and English cemeteries. Bhuj's Aina Mahal shows the court taste of the rulers of Kachchh in the 18th century. Vadodara's Laxmi Vilas Palace, finished in 1890, is one of the large princely palaces of the late 19th century. Gujarat's crafts, such as Patola weaving at Patan, Ajrakh block printing in Kachchh and Rogan painting, are living heritage you can see being made.

Coastal sites also tell the story of the sea. At Dwarka and Bet Dwarka, underwater and onshore surveys have recorded stone anchors and structures, though their dates and meaning are still debated. Students who follow such headlines may enjoy our session on whether excavation news is evidence or exaggeration.

sections.h2: Planning a heritage trip in Gujarat
paras: Ahmedabad is the natural base, with Adalaj, Lothal, Modhera and Patan as day trips. Kachchh needs its own leg: Bhuj for the Aina Mahal and museums, then Dholavira. Saurashtra (Junagadh, Somnath, Palitana) is a third. Winter is best, especially for Kachchh. Check the ASI website before you go.
Talaash Heritage runs programmes at Dholavira, Lothal and Champaner, and a multi-day [Harappan Gujarat](harappan-gujarat-cities-water-and-trade.html) study tour.

faq.q: How many UNESCO World Heritage Sites are there in Gujarat?
faq.a: Four: Champaner-Pavagadh Archaeological Park (2004), Rani ki Vav at Patan (2014), the Historic City of Ahmadabad (2017) and Dholavira, a Harappan city (2021). Lothal, the Modhera Sun Temple and several other Gujarat sites are protected nationally but are not inscribed.

faq.q: Is Lothal a UNESCO World Heritage Site?
faq.a: No. Lothal is on India's tentative list but is not inscribed. Dholavira is Gujarat's inscribed Harappan site. Lothal remains one of the most visited Harappan sites because of its basin, bead workshop and museum.

faq.q: Which are the oldest historical places in Gujarat?
faq.a: The Harappan sites of the 3rd millennium BCE are the oldest major ones: Dholavira, Lothal, Surkotada, Rangpur and Gola Dhoro. Earlier stone tool sites exist along rivers, and the Ashokan edict at Junagadh dates to the 3rd century BCE.

faq.q: Does Talaash Heritage run study tours in Gujarat?
faq.a: Yes. We run programmes at Dholavira, Lothal and Champaner, and a multi-day Harappan Gujarat study tour for schools, colleges and adult groups, arranged on request. A lecture on the first cities can be given in class before the trip.

posts.hook: A Harappan city once had a signboard.
posts.caption: At Dholavira, archaeologists found ten large Harappan signs near the north gate, likely once set on a wooden board. We still cannot read them.

posts.hook: At Rani ki Vav, walk down slowly.
posts.caption: Each level of the stepwell has its own set of carvings. Stop at every landing and look up as well as ahead.
